Content:
Suppose we have a sequence [MATH: a_i] for [MATH: i\geq 1,] and the sum of the first [MATH: 10] terms of a sequence equals [MATH: 25.] We can express this using sigma notation as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{10} a_i = 25]

Content:
If we multiply each term of the sequence by [MATH: 2,] what will be the sum of the first [MATH: 10] terms of this new sequence? In other words, what is the value of the following sum?
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{10} 2a_i]

Content:
We can compute this sum by expanding the summation:

Content:
[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(10)2a_{i}|= 2a_{1} + 2a_{2} + ⋯ + 2a_{10}; = 2 ⋅ (a_{1} + a_{2} + ⋯ + a_{10}); = 2 ⋅ ∑_(i = 1)^(10)a_{i}; = 2 ⋅ 25; = 50]

Content:
In short, we found that

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{10} 2a_i = 2\cdot \sum_{i=1}^{10} a_i .]

Content:
In general, if [MATH: a_i] is a sequence and [MATH: c] is any constant, then
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{n} c a_i = c \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i.]

If [MATH: a_i] and [MATH: b_i] for [MATH: i\geq 1] are sequences, then we have the following property:

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{n} (a_i+b_i) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i + \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i]

Content:
We sometimes call this property the sum rule.

Content:
To see how we might apply this rule, suppose we are given the following series:

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{10} a_i = 5, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{10} b_i = 8]

Content:
Let's find the value of
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{10} (2a_i-3b_i).]

Content:
First, we apply the sum rule:

Content:
[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(10)(2a_{i} − 3b_{i})|= ∑_(i = 1)^(10)(2a_{i} + (− 3b_{i})); = ∑_(i = 1)^(10)2a_{i} + ∑_(i = 1)^(10)(− 3b_{i})]

Content:
Now, recall that for any constant [MATH: c,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{n} c a_i = c \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i.]

Content:
Applying the constant multiple rule to our two series, we finally arrive at
[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(10)2a_{i} + ∑_(i = 1)^(10)(− 3b_{i})|= 2 ⋅ ∑_(i = 1)^(10)a_{i} − 3 ⋅ ∑_(i = 1)^(10)b_{i}; = 2 ⋅ 5 − 3 ⋅ 8; = − 14.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we have a sequence [MATH: a_i] for [MATH: i\geq 1,] and the sum of the first [MATH: 10] terms of a sequence equals [MATH: 25.] We can express this using sigma notation as follows:

Content:
If we multiply each term of the sequence by [MATH: 2,] what will be the sum of the first [MATH: 10] terms of this new sequence? In other words, what is the value of the following sum?
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{10} 2a_i]

Content:
We can compute this sum by expanding the summation:

Content:
